source.title: Prisma: An Open Source Toolkit for Mechanistic Interpretability in Vision and Video
source.authors: Sonia Joseph; Praneet Suresh; Lorenz Hufe; Edward Stevinson; Robert Graham; Yash Vadi; D. Bzdok; S. Lapuschkin; Lee Sharkey; Blake Richards

record.tranche_reason: The paper uses sparse autoencoders and related interpretability methods to build a vision-and-video toolkit and analyze vision models, but does not test the claimed superposition geometry or capacity account.
record.gate_note: The paper reports vision SAE sparsity and polysemanticity, but these are not tests of the listed versions: its models are vision models rather than the LLMs named in V4, and it does not measure feature overlap geometry, capacity competition, or canonicality. SAE reconstruction-loss results and toy-ViT classification accuracies do not test the claim.
record.test_reason: This is a toolkit paper. It trains and releases SAEs for vision transformers (CLIP-B, DINO-B) and reports L0, explained variance and CE-recovery metrics. It does not measure feature-overlap geometry, a sparsity-dependent transition, capacity competition, alternative causes of polysemanticity, SAE feature canonicality or stability, or feature dimensionality. Its models are vision transformers, not the LLMs V4 names. Superposition appears only as cited background (ref [19]) motivating SAEs.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors present Prisma as an open vision/video interpretability toolkit. They report that vision SAEs are much less sparse (higher L0) than language SAEs, and that SAE reconstructions can reduce model loss, especially for CLS tokens in deeper layers. They leave causes and optimal vision-SAE sparsity open.
record.recipe_differences: Applies SAE training and evaluation methods to vision models as part of a toolkit and preliminary analysis; it does not reproduce the original toy-model interventions or measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that sparsity patterns differ by token type and layer, and that the reconstruction-loss effect varies across SAE type and token configuration.

fits_no_version.finding: Vision SAEs on CLIP-B/32 and DINO-B reach high explained variance with high L0: roughly 500 to 2000 active latents per token in vanilla SAEs. Inserting SAE reconstructions sometimes lowers model CE loss (e.g. Top-K CLS layer 11, 102.97% CE recovered).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In vision transformers, SAEs recover activations with far denser codes than language SAEs, and reconstructions can act as denoisers. The bearing on superposition is undetermined.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the CVPR 2025 Workshop on Mechanistic Interpretability in Vision (MIV), Oral Presentation
record.problems: The paper describes its SAE analysis as preliminary and leaves the explanation for the vision-language sparsity difference open. Its vision SAE results do not directly test the claimed superposition geometry or capacity account.
record.rows_left_out: Layer-specific SAE evaluation-table entries in Tables 4–9 are not extracted: they report SAE reconstruction, sparsity, or loss metrics but do not test the listed superposition versions. The paper's toy-ViT classification accuracies likewise do not test superposition.

untested.parts: Toy ViTs are released but not analysed for superposition geometry, a sparsity-dependent transition or regular geometry.
No test of capacity competition or of dedicated dimensions for important features.
No test of non-capacity causes of polysemanticity.
SAEs are trained only on vision transformers, not LLMs. No measure of features spread across neurons.
No test of SAE feature completeness, stability across seeds or sizes, or canonicality.
No test of one- versus multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: The abstract says 'substantially lower sparsity patterns', but Section 5.1 shows this means higher L0 (denser codes). The SAE evaluation tables (4–9) are declared in rows_left_out and do not test any version. No verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: Toy ViTs are provided, but the paper does not test superposition geometry, a sparsity-dependent transition, or regular feature geometry in them.
Does not test whether feature competition for capacity causes polysemanticity or whether important features get dedicated dimensions.
Does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.
Measures vision-model SAEs, not indirect evidence in LLMs; it does not establish feature distribution across neurons or directions in LLMs.
Does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units of a model's representation.
Does not test whether represented features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional.

rows.subject: CLIP-B/32
rows.operation_detail: Measured average SAE L0 (active latents per token).

conditions.value: vision SAEs; approximately 500+ L0 per patch

rows.note: The paper says this L0 coexists with explained variance comparable to language SAEs. This measures vision SAE activation sparsity, not feature overlap geometry.

rows.subject: Kandinsky encoder
rows.operation_detail: Analyzed the L0 of a pretrained vision SAE.
rows.note: The paper also notes the SAE's demonstrated effectiveness for diffusion-model steering; this does not establish superposition geometry.
rows.check: The SAE analysed is a third-party pretrained SAE (Daujotas, ref [12]) on the Kandinsky encoder, not one trained by the authors. The L0 value is the authors' measurement of it. It is a sparsity statistic, not a superposition test.

rows.subject: CLIP-B/32
rows.operation_detail: Examined polysemanticity in Top-K vision SAEs.
rows.value: The paper states that the features still show polysemanticity.
rows.note: The statement groups K=64 and K=128 and gives no separate results for the two settings.
rows.check: This is a qualitative remark that Top-K (K=64,128) SAE features remain polysemantic, with no measure or numbers. It concerns SAE latents in a vision model, not neurons under capacity pressure, so it bears on no version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
